## Self-Reported Health Status

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Self-assessed health status
# Data from ABS National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Survey
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read in NATSIHS data
health_status <- f_read_natsihs_sex("Indicator_Vic_Sex_Health_Status.csv")

# Data wrangling
health_status <- health_status %>% 
  dplyr::rowwise() %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(answered_n = sum(across(excellent_n:poor_n))) %>% 
  dplyr::ungroup() %>% 
  #
  janitor::adorn_totals(fill = "Total") %>% 
  #
  dplyr::rename(verygood_n = very_good_n) %>% 
  #
  dplyr::mutate(across(excellent_n:poor_n,
                       ~ . / answered_n * 100,
                       .names = "{.col}_prop"),
                #
                answered_prop = answered_n / answered_n * 100) %>% 
  #
  dplyr::rename_with(~ stringr::str_replace(., "_n_prop$", "_prop"), ends_with("_n_prop")) %>% 
  #
  dplyr::select(sex,
                starts_with("excellent"),
                starts_with("verygood"),
                starts_with("good"),
                starts_with("fair"),
                starts_with("poor"),
                starts_with("answered")) %>% 
  #
  tidyr::pivot_longer(!sex,
                      names_to      = c("answer", ".value"),
                      names_pattern = "(.+)_(.+)") %>% 
  #
  dplyr::mutate(answer = factor(dplyr::recode(answer,
                                              "excellent" = "Excellent",
                                              "verygood"  = "Very good",
                                              "good"      = "Good",
                                              "fair"      = "Fair",
                                              "poor"      = "Poor",
                                              "answered"  = "Total"),
                                levels = c("Excellent",
                                           "Very good",
                                           "Good",
                                           "Fair",
                                           "Poor",
                                           "Total")))
```

- Data for this topic were obtained from the [2022-23 ABS National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Survey](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/aboriginal-and-torres-strait-islander-peoples/national-aboriginal-and-torres-strait-islander-health-survey/latest-release).

- Overall, 73% of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander survey respondents aged 15 years and over living in Greater Melbourne reported that they had an excellent, very good, or a good level of health. This equates to approximately 19,600 Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people in Greater Melbourne.

- Males were more likely to report an excellent level of health than females (18% vs. 6%), while females were more likely to report a poor level of health than males (10% vs. 1.4%).

::: {.callout-tip title="Definitions and notes about this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
- Data for this topic were collected from all people aged 15 years and over completing the 2022-23 ABS National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Survey.

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- `r note_aboriginality_natsihs`
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Survey questions for this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
- In general, would you say that your health is excellent, very good, good, fair, or poor?
  - `r note_response_likert_excellent`

:::

## Any Long-Term Health Condition

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Any long-term health condition, by LGA
# Data from ABS Census using TableBuilderPro
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read in Census data
condition_lga <- f_read_census_lga("Aboriginal_Health_Any_LGA.csv",
                                   variable = "any_condition") %>% 
  #
  dplyr::filter(any_condition != "Not stated")

# Data wrangling
condition_lga <- condition_lga %>%
  #
  dplyr::mutate(any_condition = dplyr::case_when(
    any_condition == "Has one or more long-term health condition(s)" ~ "yes",
    TRUE ~ "no")) %>% 
  #
  f_wrangle_census_lga(variable = any_condition,
                       level    = "person",
                       dichot   = "yes")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Any long-term health condition, by age and sex
# Data from ABS Census using TableBuilderPro
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read in Census data
condition_agesex <- f_read_census_agesex("Aboriginal_Health_Any_AgeSex.csv",
                                         variable = "any_condition") %>% 
  #
  dplyr::filter(any_condition != "Not stated")

# Data wrangling
condition_agesex <- condition_agesex %>% 
  #
  dplyr::mutate(any_condition = dplyr::case_when(
    any_condition == "Has one or more long-term health condition(s)" ~ "yes",
    TRUE ~ "no")) %>%  
  #
  f_wrangle_census_agesex(variable = any_condition,
                          dichot   = "yes")
```

- Data for this topic were obtained from the [ABS Census 2021](https://www.abs.gov.au/census).

- Overall, 43% (n = 4,850) of people living in the NEPHU catchment who identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander in the Census are living with one or more long-term health conditions. This is higher than for non-Indigenous people living in the NEPHU catchment (33%).

- The number of people living in different LGAs within the NEPHU catchment who identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander in the Census who are living with one or more long-term health conditions ranged from 850 (Whittlesea LGA) to 90 (Manningham LGA).

- The gap between the observed number of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people who were living with one or more long-term health conditions and the expected number if the proportion was the same as for non-Indigenous people was biggest for Whittlesea and Hume LGAs.

- The percentage of people living in different LGAs within the NEPHU catchment who identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander in the Census who are living with one or more long-term health conditions ranged from 47% (Maroondah LGA) to 32% (Manningham LGA).

- The percentage of people who identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander living in the NEPHU catchment who are living with one or more long-term health conditions increased with increasing age for both males and females.

- The gap between the observed number of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people who were living with one or more long-term health conditions and the expected number if the proportion was the same as for non-Indigenous people was biggest for younger people for both males and females.

::: {.callout-tip title="Definitions and notes about this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
- Data for this topic were collected from all people completing the ABS Census 2021.

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- `r note_aboriginality_census`

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- People were classified as living with a long-term health condition if they have ever been told by a doctor or nurse that they have one or more of these specified conditions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Census questions for this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
- Has the person been told by a doctor or nurse that they have any of these long-term health conditions? (*Select all that apply*)
  - Arthritis
  - Asthma
  - Cancer (including remission)
  - Dementia (including Alzheimer's)  
  - Diabetes (excluding gestational diabetes)
  - Heart disease (including heart attack or angina)
  - Kidney disease
  - Lung condition (including COPD or emphysema)
  - Mental health condition (including depression or anxiety)
  - Stroke
  - Any other long-term health condition(s)
  - No long-term health condition

:::
